promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Oct 18 2026, 2 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: Skip the 22-miler: your 20 and last Sunday's 17 are enough, and the earlier race date makes this week the start of your taper. Keep the sharp work, trim the miles, and make Sunday's 15 with a marathon-pace finish your last long run.

flags.title: Extra miles
flags.detail: Treat planned distances as limits now. Two weeks ago you added a fourth rep and ran 5 extra long-run miles. With the race on Oct 18, stop at 8 mi Wednesday and 15 mi Sunday even if you feel great.

flags.title: Heart rate caps
flags.detail: Your last two long runs averaged 146 bpm with over half the time in zone 3. Keep the first 11 miles on Sunday under 148 so the final 4 miles are the only real effort. Keep easy days under 142.

flags.title: Fuel rehearsal
flags.detail: Sunday is your last long run, so take the same gels and drink you plan to use on Oct 18. Notice how your stomach handles them at marathon pace.

flags.title: Marathon pace check
flags.detail: Aim for 8:30 to 8:35 per mile on Sunday's last 4 miles. If it feels hard in the first mile of the finish, say so in your check-in, because it changes how I set your race pace.

answers.question: The race got moved two weeks earlier, to October 18, because of the bridge works. That's three weeks from today. I've only done one 20. Do I still have time for my 22-miler?
answers.answer:
No, I would not run a 22-miler, and you do not need one. At your usual long-run pace of about 10:00 per mile it is roughly 3 hours 40 minutes on your feet, close to your whole goal time. It would also take around ten days to recover from, and that would eat into the weeks you need fresh legs.

You already have what a long run is for. The 20 on Sep 13 took 3 hours 20 minutes, and last Sunday's 17 held an even pace with only 4.7 bpm of heart-rate drift. You have also strung together four weeks of 37 to 53 miles, so the date change cost you time but not the build.

The better use of this Sunday is 15 miles with the last 4 at marathon pace. It rehearses race effort on tired legs for a fraction of the recovery cost. After that, the long run next weekend drops to about 10 easy miles on Sun Oct 11, and the volume keeps falling into race week.

new.analysis:
Last week went exactly to plan, so there is nothing to correct. All five runs were done at the planned distances, the threshold reps averaged 7:58 per mile with 1 percent fade, and the long run held 9:59 per mile from start to finish. Pain was 0/10 every day and you averaged about 7 hours of sleep.

Your easy-running share of 61 percent looks low but is not a problem. The easy days themselves were 97 to 98 percent in zone 2. The long run drifted into zone 3, and the warm-up and recoveries around the threshold reps count as harder time, which pulls the weekly share into the low 60s.

The race moving up two weeks changes the timing, not the approach. In the last three weeks before a marathon you hold the sharpness and cut the volume, so the fitness you built shows up fresh on race morning. This week is the first step: about 10 percent fewer miles than last week, the same threshold pace with less of it, and one long run that finishes at race effort.

The gap between your threshold pace and race pace is encouraging. You held 7:58 per mile for 2-mile reps with heart rate peaking at 168 of 187, and 3:45 needs about 8:34 per mile, roughly 36 seconds slower. That gives you room, though a 2-mile rep is not a marathon, which is why the final 4 miles on Sunday matter.

Holding back is the hard part of this stretch. You added miles and an extra rep two weeks ago and came through fine, but with the race this close extra miles cannot make you fitter by Oct 18. They can only leave you tired on the start line.

The nerves about the new date are understandable, and routine is the best use of them. Sleep 7 hours or more, keep Monday and Friday as true rest days, and settle your race-day shoes and fuel this week rather than leaving them to race morning.
